html:
The Book of Kings, a long epic poem in Persian written by Ferdowsi between about 977 and 1010. At some 50,000 couplets it is one of the longest poems ever written by one person, and it is the national epic of Iran and the lands of Persian culture.

It tells Iran's past from the creation of the world to the Arab conquest in the 7th century. The early parts are myth: the first kings, the war between Iran and Turan, and the hero Rostam, who unknowingly kills his own son Sohrab. The later parts move into real history with the Sasanian kings. Ferdowsi worked from older prose histories kept at the Sasanian court.

Ferdowsi spent about thirty years on it. He began under the Iranian Samanids and finished it for the Turkic ruler Mahmud of Ghazni. A well-known story says Mahmud paid him badly.

Why it matters: after the Arab conquest, Arabic became the language of religion and learning. Ferdowsi wrote in Persian with few Arabic words, and his poem helped keep the language and the memory of pre-Islamic Iran alive. Later rulers, including Turks and Mongols, paid for lavish illustrated copies to present themselves as heirs of the old kings. The Ilkhanate and Safavid shahs commissioned some of the most famous ones.
